methodological_rigor.justification: The study evaluates tumor-agnostic MRD (Guardant Reveal epigenomic/methylation-based assay) in 60 patients from the NADIM II randomized phase II trial, with 83 valid samples across three batches. Statistical approaches are rigorous: Cox proportional hazards models with Schoenfeld residuals testing for the proportional hazards assumption, Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank tests, and likelihood ratio statistics to formally quantify the added prognostic value of MRD beyond pCR—an important methodological contribution. Non-cancer-related events (COVID-19 deaths) are censored with transparency. Key limitations: small sample size (n=60 MRD-evaluable of 73 operated patients); only 7 MRD-positive patients, limiting statistical power for MRD-positive subgroup analyses; the MRD study was an exploratory objective, not pre-specified for the primary NADIM II endpoints; the control arm is small (n=15); and the study uses a tumor-agnostic assay that may have lower sensitivity than tumor-informed approaches, potentially missing MRD-positive patients and inflating apparent prognostic utility. One relapse in a serially MRD-negative patient (solitary brain metastasis) suggests CNS sanctuary effect limitations of plasma ctDNA.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a prospective exploratory analysis within a multicenter randomized phase II trial (NADIM II), mapping to LoE 2b for the parent trial with the MRD component as an exploratory endpoint. Clinical relevance is high: perioperative chemoimmunotherapy is now standard of care for resectable stage III NSCLC, and identifying non-pCR patients who have excellent prognosis without additional treatment intensification has direct implications for adjuvant de-escalation. The finding that MRD negativity in at least two samples identifies a subset of non-pCR patients with comparable outcomes to pCR patients (all alive, one relapse only) is particularly clinically actionable, potentially supporting de-escalation of adjuvant immunotherapy. However, the small sample size and exploratory design require prospective validation before practice change.

reporting_quality.justification: The study follows REMARK guidelines well: patient selection from the parent trial is documented (82.2% of operated patients; Supplementary Fig. S1), the MRD assay methodology is detailed (epigenomic methylation partitioning, >20,000 DMRs, Illumina NovaSeq, LOQ 0.01%), batch effects are assessed (consistent detection rates across three batches), statistical methods are pre-specified and appropriate, and the exploratory nature is explicitly acknowledged. MRD results for all samples are available in Supplementary Data S1. The somatic variants in MRD-positive samples are tabulated (Table 2) and concordance with tumor tissue validated in one case. COVID-19 censoring is transparently handled. Limitations of assay sensitivity relative to tumor-informed approaches and the underpowered subgroup analyses are explicitly stated.

novelty_literature.justification: The prognostic value of MRD after surgery in NSCLC is established by prior studies (TRACERx, Chaudhuri 2017, Chen 2023 using tumor-informed approaches). The novelty of this study lies in: (i) the tumor-agnostic epigenomic (methylation-based) approach in a randomized clinical trial context, providing a clinically scalable alternative to tumor-informed MRD; (ii) the use of likelihood ratio statistics to formally demonstrate that MRD adds prognostic value beyond pCR; and (iii) the finding that serial MRD negativity (≥2 samples) in non-pCR patients identifies a favorable-prognosis subgroup. These are meaningful but incremental advances in the MRD-NSCLC literature; the core concept (MRD predicts recurrence) is well-established.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is concise and well-organized, with a focused narrative from NADIM II context through MRD methodology, detection rates, prognostic analyses, and clinical implications. The use of LR statistics to formally demonstrate added value beyond pCR is well-explained. The discussion contextualizes findings within the MRD-NSCLC landscape, addresses limitations transparently (small sample size, tumor-agnostic sensitivity, exploratory design), and identifies specific clinical implications (de-escalation hypothesis, serial testing strategy). The case vignette of the single relapsing MRD-negative patient (CNS sanctuary) adds interpretive depth. Tables 1 and 2 are appropriately detailed.

key_strengths: Prospective exploratory MRD analysis within a multicenter randomized clinical trial (NADIM II) using a tumor-agnostic epigenomic assay, providing scalable real-world applicability without requiring tumor tissue
Formal likelihood ratio test demonstrating MRD adds significant prognostic value beyond pCR for both EFS (P<0.001) and OS (P=0.015), a rigorous methodological contribution

Clinically actionable finding: serial MRD negativity (≥2 samples) identifies non-pCR patients with excellent prognosis (all alive, single relapse only), potentially supporting adjuvant de-escalation trials
Transparent handling of non-cancer-related events (COVID-19), and MRD-positive somatic variant data including concordance with pretreatment tumor tissue
key_concerns: Very small sample with only 7 MRD-positive patients; key subgroup analyses (non-pCR MRD-positive vs. negative; serial MRD-negative group n=25) are critically underpowered with extremely wide CIs

Tumor-agnostic epigenomic assay has lower sensitivity than tumor-informed approaches, creating potential for false-negative MRD results that inflate the apparent excellent prognosis of MRD-negative patients
MRD was an exploratory (non-pre-specified primary) endpoint in NADIM II; the study is hypothesis-generating and subject to post-hoc selection bias in the ≥2 negative samples analysis
Control arm is very small (n=15) with MRD-positive in 3 (20%), making arm-specific MRD analyses underpowered and precluding conclusions about differential MRD utility with vs. without immunotherapy
chief_reviewer.rationale: This well-reported exploratory study provides valuable early evidence that tumor-agnostic epigenomic MRD assessment adds prognostic value beyond pCR in perioperative chemoimmunotherapy-treated NSCLC, with the serial MRD negativity finding in non-pCR patients being the most clinically actionable result; Tier 3 placement is appropriate for a methodologically sound but underpowered exploratory analysis that generates important hypotheses for prospective MRD-guided de-escalation trials.
